APPENDIX
Court of appeals order granting mandamus 
(4th Cir. Oct. 7, 2026) ......................................................................................1a
Court of appeals order denying party committees’ 
motion for stay (4th Cir. Oct. 7, 2026)...........................................................30a

FILED: October 7, 2026
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 
FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT 
No. 26-2230 
In re: SHERROD BROWN; JON OSSOFF, ROY COOPER, and KRISTEN 
MCDONALD RIVET, 
Petitioners. 
O R D E R 
KING and WYNN, Circuit Judges: 
In the face of the 2026 general election season, the Federal Communications 
Commission (the “FCC,” or the “Commission”) has endeavored to create from whole cloth 
a new rule entirely outside the purview of judicial review. Specifically, the FCC’s Media 
Bureau has extended to political parties favorable campaign advertising rates to which 
under law only the candidates themselves are statutorily entitled. And the Commission has 
since delayed agency review in an obvious effort to preclude judicial review prior to the 
November 3 election day. If allowed to continue dragging its feet, the FCC will have 
evaded meaningful judicial review of its newly created rule. The FCC’s actions are not 
only unfortunate — but also an assault on our Constitution’s separation of powers. Put 
simply, the FCC has thumbed its nose at Congress’s statutory commands and the settled 
principle of judicial review. See Marbury v. Madison, 1 Cranch 137, 177 (1803) (Marshall, 
C.J.) (“It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 1 of 29
(1a)

2 
law is.”). We have heretofore accorded the FCC a substantial amount of grace, but its 
gamesmanship must end. Consequently, as explained herein, we are obliged to grant the 
pending petition for mandamus relief. 
I. 
These mandamus proceedings are part of an ongoing dispute over who is entitled to 
the “lowest unit charge,” or “LUC,” for broadcast campaign advertisements in the run-up 
to elections. The statutory LUC requirement provides that during the 45-day period 
preceding a primary election and the 60-day period preceding a general election, “[t]he 
charges made for the use of any broadcasting station by any person who is a legally 
qualified candidate for any public office in connection with his campaign” must not exceed
“the lowest unit charge of the station for the same class and amount of time for the same 
period.” See 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)(A). Pursuant to the plain statutory language, it has 
long been understood and accepted — including by the FCC itself — that only candidates, 
that is real persons, are entitled to the LUC. 
On March 30, 2026, however, the FCC’s Media Bureau issued a “Public Notice” 
that requires broadcasters to extend the LUC to political parties engaged in coordinated 
expenditures with candidates and to joint fundraising committees with political-party and 
other non-candidate members. Although the Public Notice purports to merely restate 
previous Media Bureau guidance concerning LUC eligibility, it identifies no previous 
Media Bureau guidance specifying that non-persons and non-candidates — political parties 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 2 of 29
2a

3 
and joint fundraising committees with non-candidate members — can ever be entitled to 
the LUC. 
In the resulting dispute, the FCC is joined on one side by the intervenors National 
Republican Congressional Committee and National Republican Senatorial Committee 
(together, the “Party Committees”). On the other side are a Democratic candidate for the 
U.S. House of Representatives, Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, and three 
Democratic candidates for the U.S. Senate, Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Jon Ossoff of Georgia, 
and Roy Cooper of North Carolina (collectively, the “Federal Candidates”). 
A. 
More than five months ago, on April 29, 2026, the Federal Candidates filed an 
Application for Review with the FCC (the “Application for FCC Review,” or the 
“Application”), seeking to have the full Commission set aside the Media Bureau’s Public 
Notice. The Application argues that rather than reiterating well-settled principles, the 
Public Notice constitutes a novel statutory interpretation that is directly contradicted by 
FCC and other precedents, and that is incompatible with the plain language of the LUC 
requirement and relevant campaign finance statutes. 
The Application also addresses how the Public Notice aggrieves the Federal 
Candidates, explaining that they are in highly competitive races for U.S. House and Senate 
seats being targeted by the Party Committees; that the Party Committees are expected to 
heavily spend on advertisements opposing the Federal Candidates and supporting their 
opponents, including through coordinated expenditures and joint fundraising committee 
advertising; and that by requiring broadcasters to extend the LUC to political parties and 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 3 of 29
3a

4 
joint fundraising committees for such advertisements, the Public Notice places the Federal 
Candidates at a competitive disadvantage, forcing them to respond to a higher volume of 
opposing advertisements than otherwise could have been purchased at the same price point, 
and diluting their independent campaign messaging. 
Twice, the Application explicitly urges an expedited decision by the Commission 
given the impending November general election. Nevertheless, in the more than five 
months that have followed, the Commission has yet to resolve the Federal Candidates’ 
Application for FCC Review. 
B. 
1. 
 The Federal Candidates first turned to this Court in late June 2026, filing a Petition 
for Review in matter No. 26-1785, Brown v. FCC, and successfully moving to expedite our 
proceedings. With the support of the Party Committees, the FCC sought dismissal of the 
Petition for Review for lack of jurisdiction, principally contending that there could be no 
judicial review of the Public Notice under 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(7) until the Commission 
issues a decision on the Application for FCC Review. 
In response to the FCC’s jurisdictional contention, the Federal Candidates 
maintained that the only statutory precondition to filing their Petition for Review was first 
filing the Application for FCC Review, such that there was no need to await the 
Commission’s decision. Alternatively, the Federal Candidates asserted that because the 
Commission, up to that point, had taken no action whatsoever on the Application for FCC 
Review, the Application had been constructively denied. 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 4 of 29
4a

5 
2. 
Following the August 7, 2026, oral argument in this Court on the Federal 
Candidates’ Petition for Review — and with the matter poised for decision — the FCC 
notified us on August 17, 2026, that there had finally been a modicum of action on the 
Application for FCC Review. Specifically, the FCC advised that its Chairman had 
circulated a proposed order to his fellow Commissioners on August 14, 2026, that would 
dismiss the Federal Candidates’ Application as an “improper vehicle” for the Commission’s 
review of the Public Notice. See Brown v. FCC, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir. Aug. 17, 2026), 
ECF No. 63, at 1 (FCC’s letter to this Court under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 
28(j)). According to the FCC, the premise of the proposed order is that the Public Notice 
merely restates previous Media Bureau guidance, such that the Application would have the 
Commission improperly “revisit[] existing law on the eve of an election, after primaries 
have occurred and plans have been made for the general election based on the existing 
rules.” Id. 
Along with the proposed order dismissing the Federal Candidates’ Application, the 
FCC proffered a recent order of the Media Bureau denying a petition of the Television 
Bureau of Advertising, Inc. (“TVB”), for reconsideration of the Public Notice. See In re 
Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge for Legally Qualified Candidates for Federal Office 
and All Authorized Committees, DA 26-851, Order on Reconsideration (FCC Aug. 13, 
2026). Sticking with the FCC’s erroneous characterization of the Public Notice as a 
reiteration of previous guidance, the Media Bureau’s order asserts that “[s]uch a reminder 
is not a decision or action that can be challenged through a petition for reconsideration.” 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 5 of 29
5a

6 
Id. at 1. Once again, however, the Media Bureau failed to identify any previous FCC 
guidance stating that political parties and joint fundraising committees with non-candidate 
members can be entitled to the LUC. Instead, the order vaguely references prior 
“response[s] to informal inquiries from regulated parties.” Id. at 2. 
 One of the three FCC Commissioners dissented from the Media Bureau’s denial of 
reconsideration in the TVB matter, while also criticizing irregular processes utilized with 
respect to the Federal Candidates’ Application and the Public Notice itself. See In re 
Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge for Legally Qualified Candidates for Federal Office 
and All Authorized Committees, DA 26-851, Statement of Commissioner Anna M. Gomez 
(FCC Aug. 25, 2026). The dissent laments that “[n]othing about this proceeding was 
handled correctly.” Id. at 2. In conjunction with the dissent, the same Commissioner issued 
a public statement asserting that “[t]he American people should not have sweeping 
election-year rule changes forced on them in the dark, on the eve of an election, without a 
single opportunity for public input.” See Anna M. Gomez, FCC to Unleash Flood of Dark 
Money into Broadcast Advertising Ahead of Midterm Election, at 1 (Aug. 25, 2026).1
1
 By law, the FCC is to be comprised of five Commissioners, who are appointed by 
the President and confirmed by the Senate. See 47 U.S.C. § 154(a). No more than three 
of the five Commissioners can be members of the same political party. Id. § 154(b)(5). 
Currently, the FCC has only three Commissioners — two Republicans and one Democrat 
— meaning that the Commission has two vacancies. The dissenting Commissioner, Anna 
M. Gomez, is the lone Democrat on the Commission. 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 6 of 29
6a

7 
3. 
On August 25, 2026, this Court granted the Federal Candidates’ Petition for Review, 
setting aside and holding for naught the Public Notice. See Brown v. FCC, No. 26-1785 
(4th Cir. Aug. 25, 2026), ECF No. 66 (“Brown I”). Rejecting the FCC’s jurisdictional 
contention, we recognized that the Public Notice “constitutes a ‘final’ order because it is 
— in both substance and operation — a legislative rule, meaning that the Public Notice is 
necessarily the law of the land and final.” Id. at 15-16. 
We further recognized that by its actions — and inaction — the Commission had 
constructively denied the Federal Candidates’ Application for FCC Review and adopted 
the Media Bureau’s Public Notice. We explained:
The present circumstances readily constitute a constructive denial. 
When the Federal Candidates initiated this action on June 22, 2026, their 
Application for FCC Review was pending with the Commission for 
approximately two months. When we conducted our oral argument earlier 
this month, the Application was pending for 100 days. On September 4 — 
the date the LUC requirement becomes effective for the impending 
November election — it will be 128 days since the Federal Candidates filed 
their Application.
Despite the time-sensitive nature of these proceedings, the 
Commission intentionally took no action and offered no response to the 
Application for more than three months. The Commission did not, for 
example, seek responses from impacted parties, or engage in fact finding, or 
secure supplemental briefing, or solicit public comment, or schedule or 
conduct an oral argument. 
Meanwhile, at our oral argument, the FCC’s lawyer admitted — with 
commendable candor — that “it is very unlikely that the Commission will 
act here before September 4th.” See Oral Argument at 49:49-50:12, Brown 
v. FCC, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir. Aug. 7, 2026). Concomitantly, the lawyer also 
represented to this Court that there would be value in awaiting the 
Commission’s decision on the Public Notice’s merits and that the Public 
Notice is, in any event, absolutely correct. 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 7 of 29
7a

8 
Ten short days later, the Commission finally took some action on the 
Federal Candidates’ Application. But that action had nothing to do with 
assessing the merits of the Public Notice either by September 4, 2026, or 
ever. Rather, the FCC Chairman proposed the summary dismissal of the 
Application as unreviewable by the Commission. 
In these unusual circumstances, we are satisfied that the Commission 
has constructively denied the Application for FCC Review and thereby 
adopted the Public Notice. Cf. Friedman v. FAA, 841 F.3d 537, 542-43 (D.C. 
Cir. 2016) (finding constructive denial where the FAA “placed [the 
applicant] in a holding pattern” by refusing to issue a formal decision). The 
Public Notice is “final” for this reason. 
See Brown I at 14-15. Given our constructive denial ruling, we further recognized that “we 
need not wade into the parties’ dispute as to whether the only statutory precondition to 
filing the Petition for Review was first filing the Application for FCC Review (as the 
Federal Candidates contend), or whether 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(7) permits judicial review 
only after the Commission has ruled on the Application (as the FCC argues).” Id. at 15 
n.8. 
As for the merits of the Public Notice, we emphasized “that the legitimacy of the 
Public Notice turns on a question of pure statutory interpretation, and that our Court is 
obliged to ‘exercise [its own] independent judgment’ in conducting that review.” See 
Brown I at 18 (quoting Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024)). That 
is, we underscored that “it is ‘emphatically the province and duty of’ our Court — not the 
FCC — ‘to say what the law is.’” See id. (quoting Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 412 (quoting 
Marbury v. Madison, 1 Cranch 137, 177 (1803))). 
We then easily concluded “the LUC requirement and pertinent campaign finance 
statutes are clear that neither political parties nor joint fundraising committees with nonUSCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 8 of 29
8a

9 
candidate members can be entitled to the LUC.” See Brown I at 28-29. And we ruled that, 
“in asserting otherwise, the Public Notice is plainly contrary to law and cannot stand.” Id. 
at 29. Consequently, we granted the Federal Candidates’ Petition for Review and held for 
naught the Public Notice.
Our distinguished colleague dissented, asserting both that we lacked jurisdiction to 
review the Public Notice and that the Public Notice is correct on the merits. On the latter 
issue, the dissent relied on a First Amendment theory not raised by the FCC or Party 
Committees. See Brown I at 40 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting) (introducing the theory that “the 
First Amendment would disfavor [the Federal Candidates’] view of [what the dissent 
deemed to be] ambiguous statutory text”). 
On August 26, 2026, the Party Committees moved to stay the issuance of the Brown 
I mandate, pending disposition of a petition for writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court. On 
August 27, 2026, this Court denied the Party Committees’ motion and directed the clerk to 
immediately issue the mandate.
C. 
On August 28, 2026, the Party Committees filed an emergency application in the 
Supreme Court for a stay of our Brown I mandate pending the filing and disposition of a 
petition for a writ of certiorari. By an opinion of September 4, 2026, the Supreme Court 
granted the requested stay and recalled our mandate. See Nat’l Republican Congressional 
Comm. v. Brown, No. 26A274 (U.S. Sept. 4, 2026) (per curiam) (“Brown II”). In doing so, 
the Court concluded that the Party Committees showed “(1) a reasonable probability that 
four Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 9 of 29
9a

10 
prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the judgment below; and (3) a 
likelihood that irreparable harm will result from the denial of a stay.” Id. at 2 (quoting 
Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam)). 
The Court specified that “the first and second stay factors weigh in favor of granting 
the application,” in that “the Fourth Circuit likely lacked statutory jurisdiction to address 
[the Federal Candidates’] challenge.” See Brown II at 3. Without addressing our ruling 
that the Commission constructively denied the Federal Candidates’ Application for FCC 
Review, the Court concluded that “the Communications Act makes clear that an aggrieved 
party must wait for the Commission to resolve its application for review by order before 
filing a petition for judicial review.” Id. at 2. Key to the Court’s conclusion was that “[t]he 
Commission is required to resolve every application it receives.” Id. at 3 (citing 47 U.S.C. 
§ 155(c)(4)). The Court summarized that “[t]he Communications Act thus contemplates 
that an aggrieved party will file an application for review with the Commission, that the 
Commission will resolve that application by order, and that public notice of that order will 
issue before an aggrieved party may petition for further review in federal court.” Id.
With respect to the third factor, the Court considered the likelihood of irreparable 
harm to only the Party Committees. See Brown II at 3. In ruling in favor of the Party 
Committees on this stay factor, the Court explained: 
They represent that, in light of the Fourth Circuit’s decision — which the 
Fourth Circuit likely lacked jurisdiction to issue — broadcasters are already 
rescinding favorable rates. Current and future rescissions will require the 
[Party Committees] to pay more for advertising space, thereby hampering 
their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the 
midterms. That injury, which implicates their First Amendment rights to 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 10 of 29
10a

11
speak and coordinate their political activities freely, cannot be remedied after 
the fact through refunds or reimbursements. 
Id. at 3-4 (citing Nat’l Republican Senatorial Comm. v. FEC, 146 S. Ct. 2404 (2026)). 
Since the Supreme Court’s stay, the Commission has neither entered its proposed dismissal 
order circulated by the FCC Chairman on August 14, 2026, nor otherwise resolved the 
Federal Candidates’ Application.
D. 
On September 8, 2026, the Federal Candidates commenced the present action by 
filing a petition for a writ of mandamus, requesting that this Court order the Commission 
to decide the still-pending Application for FCC Review. See In re Brown, No. 26-2230 
(4th Cir. Sept. 8, 2026), ECF No. 2 (the “Mandamus Petition”). The Federal Candidates 
explain therein that they “bring this [Mandamus Petition] to address the Supreme Court’s 
jurisdictional concern and enable a decisive ruling on the validity of the Public Notice 
before it is too late to matter.” Id. at 1. As the Federal Candidates put it, “[m]andamus is 
urgently needed to prevent ongoing statutory violations and irreparable harm that th[is] 
Court already recognized in Brown I.” Id. at 14. 
We again expedited our proceedings, but this time over the dissent of our good 
colleague. See In re Brown, No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Sept. 9, 2026), ECF No. 12. He preferred 
to immediately deny the Mandamus Petition on the premise that “[t]he Supreme Court’s 
[Brown II] stay order stressed the importance of not keeping matters in a continually 
unsettled state in the ‘critical weeks leading up to the midterms.’” Id. at 2 (quoting Brown 
II at 3). The dissent thereby mischaracterizes Brown II’s discussion of the likelihood of 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 11 of 29
11a

12 
irreparable harm to the Party Committees in the “critical weeks leading up to the midterms” 
as being an admonition to hold the Public Notice sacrosanct for the November 2026 general 
election. 
Nearly five months after the Federal Candidates filed their Application for FCC 
Review, and just hours before the FCC’s response to the Mandamus Petition was due, the 
Media Bureau issued a public notice on September 15, 2026, seeking comment on the 
Federal Candidates’ Application through September 30, 2026. In its response to the 
Mandamus Petition, the FCC asserts that it had just solicited public comment “in response 
to statements by this Court and one of the Commissioners that the agency had not solicited 
[such] comment.” See In re Brown, No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Sept. 15, 2026), ECF No. 21, at 
3 (referring to, inter alia, our mention in Brown I of soliciting public comment as an 
example of actions not taken in the months after the Application was filed). Representing 
that therefore the “‘agency process’ remains ongoing” and that “[t]he Commission requires 
the opportunity to consider comments submitted by interested parties before it issues an 
order addressing the [Federal Candidates’ Application],” the FCC contends that mandamus 
relief is unwarranted. Id.
In their reply of September 17, 2026, the Federal Candidates refer to the FCC’s 
solicitation of public comment as “a farce” and as confirmation “that the Commission’s 
only goal is to postpone judicial review by any means necessary.” See In re Brown, No. 
26-2230, at 2 (4th Cir. Sept. 17, 2026), ECF No. 25. The reply elaborates that “[i]t is only 
now, having obtained a Supreme Court stay that heads off the risk of pre-election judicial 
review in the absence of a final Commission order, that the Commission is suddenly back 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 12 of 29
12a

13 
to insisting that it needs more time — with the request for public comment serving as the 
fig leaf for that insistence.” Id. at 4. 
On September 18, 2026, however, we accorded grace to the FCC and deferred action 
on the Mandamus Petition until at least October 1, 2026. See In re Brown, No. 26-2230 
(4th Cir. Sept. 18, 2026), ECF No. 27. In so doing, we reminded the parties that under 47 
U.S.C. § 155(c)(4), the Commission “is required to resolve every application it receives.” 
Id. at 1 (quoting Brown II at 3). We further reminded the parties “that by statute, the 
Commission is required to conduct its business ‘prompt[ly] . . . with the objective of 
rendering a final decision (1) within three months from the date of filing in all original 
application . . . cases in which it will not be necessary to hold a hearing, and (2) within six 
months from the final date of the hearing in all hearing cases.’” Id. at 1-2 (alterations in 
original) (quoting 47 U.S.C. § 155(d)). Our good colleague again dissented, once more 
expressing a preference to deny the Mandamus Petition “forthwith” and asserting that the 
Supreme Court instructed us in Brown II “that matters should be left in a stable state ‘in 
the critical weeks leading up to the midterms.’” Id. at 3 (quoting Brown II at 3). 
That brings us to October 1, 2026, when the FCC informed us that it has now 
solicited public comment in the related TVB matter, such that we should “further defer[]” 
these mandamus proceedings, if not outright deny the Mandamus Petition. See In re 
Brown, No. 26-2230, at 2 (4th Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), ECF No. 28 (FCC’s letter to this Court 
under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 28(j)). As related by the FCC, on September 
14, 2026, TVB filed an application for review of the Media Bureau’s denial of 
reconsideration of the Public Notice, and on September 30, 2026, the FCC invited comment 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 13 of 29
13a

14 
on the TVB application through October 19, 2026. The FCC now contends that because 
there are “substantially overlap[ping]” issues between that application and the Federal 
Candidates’ Application, the Commission should be accorded even more time to issue a
decision on the Federal Candidates’ Application so that it can “address the [applications] 
jointly.” Id. at 1-2. 
In response, the Federal Candidates assert that “the Commission seems again to 
have unnecessarily delayed its proceedings.” See In re Brown, No. 26-2230, at 1 (ECF No. 
29 (Federal Candidates’ response to FCC’s Rule 28(j) letter). The Federal Candidates 
emphasize that “TVB filed its [application] on September 14, before FCC opened public 
comment on the [Federal Candidates’ Application].” Id. “Yet FCC waited until September 
30 to open a new comment period on the ‘substantially overlap[ping]’ issues in TVB’s 
[application].” Id. at 1-2 (first alteration in original). Addressing “[t]he new comment 
deadline [of] October 19,” the Federal Candidates characterize it as “past any window for 
meaningful judicial relief this election.” Id. at 2. The Federal Candidates thus implore this 
Court to immediately grant the Mandamus Petition. 
II. 
 The All Writs Act provides this Court with jurisdiction to issue “all writs necessary 
or appropriate.” See 28 U.S.C. § 1651. We have consistently recognized that writs of 
mandamus have “long been reserved for extraordinary cases,” where a petitioner “has no 
other adequate means to obtain relief.” See South Carolina v. United States, 907 F.3d 742, 
754 (4th Cir. 2018) (citation modified). Nevertheless, “courts may calibrate their discretion 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 14 of 29
14a

15 
to issue the writ and act more aggressively when the circumstances warrant it.” See Brown 
I at 49 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). To obtain a writ of mandamus, the petitioner must 
demonstrate “a clear and indisputable right to the relief sought and show that the 
responding party has a clear duty to do the specific act requested.” See South Carolina, 
907 F.3d at 754 (citation modified). Finally, after weighing the equities, a court must 
exercise its discretion and “be satisfied that the writ is appropriate under the 
circumstances.” Id. 
III. 
 The extraordinary circumstances of these proceedings readily demand that the 
Federal Candidates are immediately entitled to mandamus relief. Simply put, the FCC’s 
professed need for further deliberation of the Federal Candidates’ challenge to the Public 
Notice rings hollow, and our willingness to tolerate the FCC’s delay tactics is at an end. 
See Dep’t of Com. v. New York, 588 U.S. 752, 785 (2019) (recognizing that in reviewing 
agency action, a court is “not required to exhibit a naivete from which ordinary citizens are 
free”). 
First of all, at this critical juncture, the Federal Candidates have no other adequate 
remedy through which they could obtain relief. That is so because, by staying on 
jurisdictional grounds this Court’s mandate in Brown I, which set aside and held for naught 
the Public Notice, the Supreme Court has kept the Public Notice in effect. With the Public 
Notice still in effect, political parties are continuing to secure discounted LUC advertising 
rates in contravention of 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)(A)’s plain statutory text. Furthermore, the 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 15 of 29
15a

16 
Public Notice constitutes a final order of the Commission, see Brown I at 15-16, so a claim 
for unlawful agency delay under the Administrative Procedure Act is unavailable. See 
South Carolina, 907 F.3d at 759 (“An action that is ‘delayed’ rather than ‘withheld’ is not 
generally a ‘final action’ that can be addressed under the APA.” (citation modified)). 
Second, the Federal Candidates have demonstrated that they have a clear right to 
relief and that the Commission has a clear duty to act on the Application. As the Supreme 
Court recognized in Brown II, 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(4) explicitly requires that the 
Commission “shall pass upon” every application for review. See Brown II at 3; see also
South Carolina, 907 F.3d at 756 (explaining that “the word ‘shall’ usually creates a 
mandate” indicating a nondiscretionary duty to perform). Moreover, the Commission is 
obligated to enter orders that are “necessary or appropriate to expedite the prompt and 
orderly conduct of the business of the Commission with the objective of rendering a final 
decision . . . within three months” from when an application for review is filed. See 47 
U.S.C. § 155(d). 
Yet more than five months have passed since the Federal Candidates filed their 
Application for FCC Review, and nearly two months have passed since the FCC’s 
Chairman circulated his proposed order to the Commission disposing of the Application. 
This proposed order does not even address the merits of the Application — it would simply 
dismiss the Application as an improper vehicle. As the Federal Candidates have correctly 
highlighted for us, “[t]he Commission has made its decision — it simply must publish the 
order.” See Mandamus Petition 18. Moreover, the Commission is not legally obligated to 
explain or justify its decision on the merits of the Application. See 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(5) 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 16 of 29
16a

17 
(“In passing upon applications for review, the Commission may grant, in whole or in part, 
or deny such applications without specifying any reasons therefor.”). The Federal 
Candidates have thus demonstrated that they have a clear right to relief and that the 
Commission possesses a clear and specific statutory duty to act. 
We have highlighted the extraordinary circumstances here — circumstances that the 
FCC has been fully aware of since the Federal Candidates filed their Application. 
Approximately seven months before the November 2026 general election — the same 
election for which the Federal Candidates seek relief — the FCC’s Media Bureau issued 
its Public Notice, unlawfully extending the LUC to political parties in the critical period 
leading up to the election. Less than a month later, the Federal Candidates filed their 
Application for FCC Review. And despite its illegal expansion of the LUC from solely 
candidates to include political parties, the Commission has left the Application unresolved.
The FCC argues that the LUC should not be disturbed in the face of an impending 
election. But that contention is entirely irreconcilable with the reality that the Public 
Notice’s stated purpose was to address the impending election. If this Court were to accept 
the FCC’s position that mandamus is not available in this situation, the FCC could issue 
any rule regarding the LUC — without respect to its lawfulness — and be shielded from 
judicial review. We are unable to accept the proposition that mandamus is unavailable in 
these circumstances. As the Federal Candidates have carefully explained, they “are 
candidates in this year’s election — they cannot recover the fair competitive opportunities 
they are losing while the Commission withholds its final order.” See Mandamus Petition 
20. 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 17 of 29
17a

18 
Finally, the procedural posture of this matter weighs heavily in favor of issuing a 
mandamus writ. As we recognized in Brown I, “the legitimacy of the Public Notice turns 
on a question of pure statutory interpretation.” See Brown I at 18. As a result, we need not 
accord any deference to the Commission in this regard. Notwithstanding the view of the 
Commission majority, we are obliged to review and resolve the statutory interpretation 
question ourselves. Id. (underscoring that “it is ‘emphatically the province and duty of’ 
our Court — not the FCC — ‘to say what the law is’” (quoting Loper Bright Enters. v. 
Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024) (quoting Marbury v. Madison, 1 Cranch 137, 177 
(1803)))). And in a matter of pure statutory interpretation, the equities readily favor an 
award of mandamus relief and a prompt resolution of the Application.2
2 In dissenting from this award of mandamus relief, our distinguished colleague
repeats his mischaracterization of the Supreme Court’s stay order as “embrac[ing] what the 
Supreme Court has long emphasized: the need to preserve settled understandings prior to 
an election, here, in the ‘critical weeks leading up to the midterms.’” See post 25

WYNN, J., concurring in the order granting mandamus: 
When the question proves inconvenient, change it. That is the course our dissenting 
colleague takes today. The dissent asks whether we owe respect to the Supreme Court. Of 
course we do. But that proposition, beyond dispute, does not resolve the question before 
us. Respect for the judicial hierarchy does not release an administrative agency from its 
obligation to obey Congress.
The question is whether the Federal Communications Commission may withhold 
the decision necessary for judicial review while its disputed interpretation sets the terms of 
an election. Congress’s command cannot depend upon an unelected agency’s willingness 
to open the courthouse door. Yet that is the practical consequence of the dissent’s position.
The blueprint is simple. The Commission’s Media Bureau announces what a 
congressional statute means. Regulated parties must order their affairs accordingly. Those 
who object are told that they must first seek review by the full Commission. The 
Commission then delays its decision while the election approaches. And when the time for 
effective relief has nearly run, the expectations formed under the disputed interpretation 
become a reason to leave it undisturbed. 
What was once too early to review has become too late to remedy. The agency need 
never establish that its reading of the statute is right. It need only wait until the statute’s 
protection has lost its practical worth. 
Congress did not create an administrative process in which the agency holds both 
the power to impose an interpretation and the power to prevent its timely examination. 
Today’s writ requires the Commission to make the decision through which the controversy 
USCA4 Appeal: 26-2230 Doc: 30 Filed: 10/07/2026 Pg: 20 of 29
20a

21 
may properly reach a reviewing court. It leaves the substance of that decision where 
Congress placed it: with the Commission in the first instance. 
That distinction answers the dissent’s principal objection. The Supreme Court 
stayed our earlier mandate and explained that the pending application likely deprived this 
court of statutory jurisdiction to review the challenged notice. That order binds us. We may 
not revive our earlier merits judgment under another name. 
But requiring the Commission to decide the application does not evade the 
prerequisite the Supreme Court identified. It requires the Commission to fulfill it. The stay 
remains controlling. Any later request for judicial relief must satisfy the applicable 
jurisdictional and equitable requirements on its own terms. Nothing in today’s writ 
prejudges those questions. 
The dissent would turn a prerequisite to judicial review into a means of preventing 
review. A requirement that the Commission first act becomes a license for the Commission 
not to act. The Supreme Court’s order warrants no such conclusion. 
Congress imposed obligations on both sides of the administrative process. An 
aggrieved party must seek Commission review. The Commission, in turn, must pass upon 
the application. 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(4). The agency cannot demand obedience to the first 
obligation while treating the second as a matter of indefinite convenience. The 
Administrative Procedure Act likewise requires an agency to conclude matters presented 
to it within a reasonable time. 5 U.S.C. § 555(b). These duties belong to the statutory 
scheme no less than the requirement of administrative review itself.

What constitutes a reasonable time must account for what time takes away. An 
election affords a finite opportunity to speak, to purchase advertising, and to answer an 
opponent. Once that opportunity passes, a decision may resolve the legal question and yet
afford scant relief to those whose rights were at stake. The calendar is therefore no 
incidental feature of this dispute. Counting months tells us little unless we also consider 
what those months consume. 
Our dissenting colleague emphasizes that the earlier proceedings complicated the 
Commission’s position and that the agency has since opened an expedited comment period. 
Those circumstances deserve consideration. Agencies must have an adequate opportunity 
to deliberate, and courts should not mistake every intervening procedural step for evasion. 
But a new round of procedure does not discharge the duty to decide. Activity and 
resolution are different things. The relevant inquiry concerns the proceeding as a whole: 
whether the Commission has had a reasonable opportunity to address the application, and 
whether a concrete deadline can preserve meaningful review while allowing the agency to 
complete its work. The statutory obligation cannot recede each time another procedural 
stage begins. 
The dissent’s concern for settled expectations also carries weight. Candidates and 
broadcasters must plan their conduct, and judicial intervention near an election may impose 
real costs. But those considerations cannot automatically place an administrative
interpretation beyond the reach of the legislation it purports to administer. 
Otherwise, delay becomes its own justification. The longer the agency’s 
interpretation governs conduct, the more reliance it produces. The more reliance it

produces, the stronger the argument against examining it in time to provide effective relief. 
An interpretation thus acquires practical immunity through the very delay that shields it 
from review. Congress’s enactment becomes subordinate to the expectations generated by 
the agency’s disputed account of it. 
The danger is structural. It requires no attribution of partisan motive, and it would 
be no less troubling if the candidates who benefited were different. An unelected agency 
should not possess the practical authority to determine the conditions of electoral 
competition while also controlling whether its interpretation can receive timely judicial 
scrutiny. The distribution of that power matters whatever its immediate political 
consequences. 
We are accustomed to debating whether courts have intruded too far upon the 
legislative domain. Here we confront a different prospect: an agency escaping both 
legislative constraint and effective judicial review through its control of procedure. 
Congress supplies the governing text. The agency supplies an interpretation. And then the 
agency decides whether a court may examine that interpretation before its consequences 
have become irreversible. 
That arrangement gives administrative delay a force Congress did not confer upon 
it. 
The writ preserves the arrangement Congress did establish. The Commission must 
issue a disposition. It remains free to determine the substance of that disposition. A court 
may review it when the statutory conditions for review have been satisfied. The Supreme

Court’s stay remains undisturbed, and the requirements governing any subsequent judicial 
relief remain fully applicable. 
Each institution thus performs its assigned task. The Commission decides. The

responsibility.

WILKINSON, Circuit Judge, dissenting: 
Litigants far and wide will be eager to purchase the majority’s new board game: 
Make The Supreme Court Say It Twice. Once is enough for me, so I vote to deny the 
petition for a writ of mandamus. 
The grant of a writ of mandamus is a direct affront to the Supreme Court’s stay order
in this case. That order embraced what the Supreme Court has long emphasized: the need 
to preserve settled understandings prior to an election, here, in the “critical weeks leading 
up the midterms.” National Republican Congressional Committee v. Brown, No. 26A274, 
609 U.S. __ (2026) (slip op. at 3). The majority has now ignored the Supreme Court’s 
concern and unraveled its work. I respectfully dissent.
The timing of the majority’s egregious intrusion into the nation’s electoral process 
has made no difference to the majority at all. Its decision is “chaotic with a capital C.” In 
re Brown, No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Sept. 18, 2026) (Wilkinson, J., dissenting from order 
deferring proceedings) (slip op. at 3). After this court’s earlier decision in this case, 
broadcasters began “rescinding favorable rates” for political advertising. NRCC, 609 U.S. 
__ (2026) (slip op. at 3). Presumably they have returned to their prior contractual 
agreements after the Supreme Court’s stay. The downstream effects of this writ may force 
them to flip again. Neither parties nor candidates nor broadcasters have any idea how to 
plan, contractually or otherwise, for the rest of the election season. Any unlawful expenses 
incurred “cannot be remedied after the fact through refunds or reimbursements.” Id. at 4. 
Who can tally the intangible damage of election seasons thrown into limbo?
